Hi Samira / Mike —

Thanks again for the time yesterday. To make sure the Dedicated proposal maps cleanly to your SLA asks, can you confirm the production workload shape and the SLO targets we discussed? Specifically we need:

- a 2‑week sample of request traces (or a CSV with per-minute RPS and tokens/request)

If you can attach the CSV, we’ll run an initial sizing pass today and share a compact plan (GPU SKU + slab counts, quantization options, pre-warm strategy).

Thanks for the trace, Samira — I ran a quick sizing pass against the CSV and sketched the numbers below. This is an initial model-focused view (assumes CLS-like causal decoder; figures approximate):

Summary (conservative):
- Effective tokens/sec requirement at peak (system aggregate): ~310 RPS * 420 tokens/request / avg completion duration factor => ~130k tokens/sec
- Working-hours sustained baseline (~90% of peak windows): 95k tokens/sec
- Target P95 latency: 450 ms => target per-token processing budget ~0.0035s/token (~3.5 ms/token) for the chosen model family

GPU slab recommendations (options):
- Option A (A100 80GB, quantized FP16 + KV cache): 12 GPUs (3 slabs of 4 GPUs) providing ~140–160k tokens/sec aggregate and ~25% headroom for bursts; expected p95 compute-only latency ~320–380 ms depending on prompt lengths
- Option B (H100 80GB, AVX HVX + better sparse kernels): 8 GPUs (2 slabs of 4 GPUs) — higher per-GPU throughput; estimated tokens/sec 160–180k and p95 compute latency ~250–320 ms; allows smaller slab footprint but higher reserved cost

Operational notes / mitigations:
- KV cache warm-up: cold-starts add substantial tail. Recommend pre-warming by replaying top 5% prefixes during canary windows and a short-lived cache-reserve on each slab after deploy
- Batching profile: continuous batching will help if request coalescing latency budget exists; we assumed batching factor of 1.8 in the above numbers (observed in your CSV during 3–5min bursts)
- Quantization: moving to 4-bit quantization could increase slab capacity ~20–30% but needs model validation for hallucination risk on summarization flows
- Fallback: keep a distilled 7B variant on cheaper slab for up to 2% requests to guarantee overall availability cost tradeoffs

Preliminary SLO fit: both options meet P95 target if deployed with pre-warm and our suggested headroom. H100 option gives more comfortable latency headroom but at higher unit cost; A100 option is more predictable on reserved marketplaces.

I'll attach the Excel with per-GPU token/sec curve and assumptions. Next ask: do you want a conservative commit (A) or aggressive (B)? For proposal docs I'll convert these into committed slab counts + pricing estimate.

- Karthik
Senior Solutions Architect
Redwood Inference

Attachments: alderhealth-gpu-plan-v1.xlsx (spreadsheet, per-GPU curves and assumptions)

From: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Throughput verification and GPU slab mapping for AlderHealth v1 commit

Samira / team — quick operational addendum from the deal/ops side: 

- Canary / pilot: recommend a 2-week canary with a single slab (4 GPUs) representing ~35% of the pilot traffic and a scheduled scale to the committed slab on day +10 if metrics look good. Canary gives us real-world cold-starts and KV-warm metrics.
- Burst entitlement: include an agreed burst pool (token-based) that can be consumed for unexpected spikes; we typically set the burst pool to ~20% of monthly committed tokens to avoid immediate throttling during onboarding spikes.
- Cost-control: enable a model-variant routing policy for low-priority background jobs so you don't burn dedicated capacity on non-critical workloads.
- Contract ask: if AlderHealth is comfortable with a 12-month commit on Option A, we can lock pricing and include one free escalation playbook run during onboarding.

If you're comfortable, Marissa and I will draft the commitment appendix with slab diagrams and the canary gating thresholds.

Ben Carter
Director, Customer Success
Redwood Inference
